title: Nawab Kapur Singh
hook: offered a Mughal title, the Khalsa gave it to a man who was fanning the sangat, and he accepted humbly

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Diwali permit, and Bhai Mani Singh, who warned the Sikhs away and paid with his life. Your line was he kept faith. Today, a gentler scene, and a fan.

A hot day. The sangat sits together at Amritsar, and the air barely moves. At the edge of the gathering, one man stands with a large hand fan, slowly moving the air over everyone else. Nobody asked him to. It's his seva, his service. Meanwhile a messenger has arrived from Lahore with an astonishing offer from the governor: an estate, a robe of honor, and the title of Nawab, a lord. The Khalsa has to decide who, if anyone, will wear it.
screen: `A HOT DAY. A MAN WITH A FAN.` → `AN OFFER FROM LAHORE.` → `WHO WILL WEAR THE TITLE?`

segments.voice: Why would a governor who had hunted the Sikhs offer them a title? Tradition says force had not worked, so he tried another way: give them land and rank, and perhaps they would settle down and stop resisting. The Khalsa met to discuss it. Some wanted no title from the government that had killed their people; others saw a chance for a little breathing room. And the leaders who were asked to take it, tradition says, turned it down. So the gathering made a remarkable decision: the title would go to the one doing seva. They looked around, and there was Kapur Singh, still fanning the sangat. Not the loudest, not the most powerful, but the one with the fan in his hand. Kapur Singh did not grab it. Tradition says he would accept the robe of honor only after it had been touched to the feet of five respected Sikhs, as if to say the honor belonged to the Khalsa and he was only carrying it. And he asked one more thing: that being a nawab would never excuse him from his old service. Some tellings say his seva was cleaning the stables and tending the horses, and he kept at it. He went on to become a leader of the whole Khalsa, organizing it in the hard years ahead. But the story keeps the fan in its first scene. Seva means selfless service, and the tradition holds that it is the root leadership grows from, not a step to climb past.
screen: `A GOVERNOR'S OFFER: LAND AND A TITLE.` · `THE LEADERS TURN IT DOWN.` · `GIVE IT TO THE ONE DOING SEVA.` · `TOUCHED TO THE FEET OF FIVE SIKHS.` · then, large: `THE HUMBLE NAWAB.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person in your life who is under pressure right now, tired, stretched, overheated in some way, and ask what a fan would look like for them: a glass of water brought without asking, a chore taken off their list, ten quiet minutes to rest. Picture yourself doing it without needing them to notice, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
Kapur Singh. The Sikh who was fanning the sangat when the Khalsa chose him for a governor's title, and who took it only on condition he could keep serving.
Your line: the humble nawab. The title found the man with the fan. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Nawab Kapur Singh as a lesson in seva, and gurdwara volunteers still serve the sangat in small ways, including fanning, sweeping and cleaning shoes.
